notes.written: Written 31 Oct 2026. Figures in the tables update automatically; these summaries are refreshed separately.
themes: Brent’s expiring contract settled at $117.64 on 30 Oct and WTI at $104.12, both up about 14–15% in October. Houthi attacks on Saudi refineries, a tanker hit in the Strait of Hormuz and fears of US strikes on Iran after the 3 Nov US midterm elections drove the rise. Qatar-led talks between the US and Iran are the main hope for calm.
Decision week: one rise, one surprise, three holds

The Bank of Canada raised to 2.50%, its first rise since 2023. The Fed (10–2, two wanted a rise), ECB (unanimous) and Bank of Japan (8–1, one wanted a rise) held but all said inflation is too high. New Zealand surprised by holding in a 4–3 vote when a rise was expected.
Next week: Australia and the UK expected to raise

After Australian inflation jumped to 4.3%, all four big Australian banks expect the RBA to raise to 4.85% on 3 Nov, and markets priced about 90% odds. Markets see a Bank of England rise to 4.00% on 5 Nov as near-certain.
The US is growing fast, with inflation still high

US growth hit 3.4% (annual pace) in Q3, but the Fed’s preferred inflation measure (PCE) rose to 3.6% in September. Markets put the chance of a Fed rise in December at about 85%. The 10-year yield is near 5%, about 2.6% after inflation.

Canada’s economy was flat in August and probably shrank 0.1% in September. The euro area grew 0.4% in Q3, but France shrank and unemployment rose to 6.5%. China’s official factory index fell to 49.3 in October (below 50 means shrinking).

High real yields and rate-rise bets keep weighing on metals that pay no interest. Gold is around $4,030, down about 13% in six months, and has dipped below $4,000 at times; silver is around $52, down about 29%.

USD.note: Held at 3.75–4.00% on 28 Oct in a 10–2 vote; two members (Cook and Hammack) wanted a rise. Chair Warsh made no promises, but markets put the chance of a rise on 9 Dec at about 85%.

EUR.note: Held on 29 Oct (deposit rate 2.50%) after two rises this year. Lagarde did not rule out more rises, saying “the direction of travel is clear”; December brings new forecasts. She will step down early, on 7 Feb 2027.

GBP.note: Held at 3.75% on 17 Sep, but 3 of 9 members voted to raise to 4%. With inflation at 3.5% and a calm Budget behind it, markets see a rise on 5 Nov as near-certain.

JPY.note: Held at 1.25% on 30 Oct in an 8–1 vote (one member wanted a rise). It said underlying inflation has reached its 2% target and raised its price forecasts; many economists now see December as a real chance for the next rise.

CAD.note: Raised to 2.50% on 28 Oct, its first rise since July 2023, as oil pushes inflation up (it expects about 3.5% by year-end). Governor Macklem said more rises are likely if inflation comes in as expected or higher.

AUD.note: Raised to 4.60% on 29 Sep and said it could go further. After inflation jumped to 4.3%, a rise to 4.85% on 3 Nov is widely expected.

NZD.note: Surprised markets by holding at 2.75% on 28 Oct in a 4–3 vote (three wanted a rise). It still expects to raise rates later, and most banks expect a rise on 9 Dec.

CHF.note: Held at 0% on 24 Sep and stands ready to sell francs if needed. Inflation has crept up to the 1% mid-point of its 0–2% range; the next decision is in December.

CNY.note: Lending rates unchanged again on 20 Oct (1-year 3.00%); growth support comes mostly from the government, and some economists are calling for more after weak October surveys.

stories.USD: The economy grew at a strong 3.4% annual pace in the third quarter, above the 3.2% expected, as shoppers kept spending. But inflation is too high: the Fed’s preferred measure (PCE) rose to 3.6% in September, or 3.1% without food and energy. The Fed held at 3.75–4.00% on 28 October, yet two members wanted a rise and markets put the chance of a December rise at about 85%. Hiring is the weak spot (only 29,000 jobs in September, unemployment 4.2%), though consumer confidence jumped to 91.7 from 81.2. The 10-year yield is near 5%, about 2.6% after inflation. Next: factory survey (ISM) 2 Nov, midterm elections 3 Nov, services survey 4 Nov, October jobs report 6 Nov (63,000 expected).
stories.EUR: Euro-area inflation hit 3.8% in September, mostly from energy (up 18.9% on a year); without energy it is 2.3%. The ECB held its deposit rate at 2.50% on 29 October, unanimously, but Lagarde did not rule out a December rise, when new forecasts arrive. She also announced she will leave early, on 7 February 2027. Growth beat forecasts at 0.4% in Q3, but France shrank 0.1%, unemployment rose to 6.5% and French borrowing costs near 5% are a worry. German inflation fell to 2.8% in October, from 3.3%, thanks to a renewed fuel discount. Next: October inflation 4 Nov (4.0% expected), Lagarde speaks 5 Nov, retail sales 6 Nov.
stories.GBP: Inflation is 3.5% (September), with core at 2.8%, and markets see a Bank of England rise to 4.00% on 5 November as near-certain; three of nine members already voted for a rise in September. Chancellor John Healey’s first Budget on 28 October calmed markets: borrowing matched forecasts and gilt yields barely moved. It offered help with energy costs (a £100 payment for many households from January, the fuel duty cut extended) and raised taxes on banks and on property and savings income. The budget watchdog (OBR) sees inflation averaging 3.5% in 2027 and growth of 1.2% this year. Shoppers are cautious (retail sales −0.4%, confidence −24), but the pound hit a 19-month high against the euro. Next: Bank of England decision and new forecasts 5 Nov.
stories.JPY: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% on 30 October, but one member voted for a rise and the bank said underlying inflation has now reached its 2% target. It raised its price forecasts and will sell its stock-market funds (ETFs) faster. Many economists now see December as a real chance for the next rise, and the yen firmed after the decision. National core inflation is 2.1% and Tokyo’s early October reading 2.6%. Jobs are plentiful (unemployment 2.4%), but retail sales growth slowed to 2.3%, well below the 3.3% expected, and households are still cutting back. Dearer energy keeps the trade balance in deficit. Next: Japan holiday 3 Nov, wage data 5 Nov (UK evening), Governor Ueda speaks 6 and 7 Nov.
stories.CAD: The Bank of Canada raised its rate to 2.50% on 28 October, its first rise since July 2023, because high oil prices are pushing inflation up (3.1% in September) and it expects about 3.5% by year-end. Governor Macklem said more rises are likely if inflation comes in as expected or higher. Yet the economy is stalling: GDP was flat in August, an early estimate shows a 0.1% fall in September, and growth over the third quarter was only about 0.3%. Underlying inflation is under 2% (median 1.9%), and 68,300 jobs were lost in September (unemployment 6.5%). High oil does help exports. Next: Macklem speaks 3 and 5 Nov, trade 4 Nov, federal budget 5 Nov (UK evening), October jobs 6 Nov.
stories.AUD: Inflation jumped to 4.3% in the year to September, from 4.0% and above the 4.2% expected, driven by housing (+5.2%) and fuel. The core measure the RBA watches (trimmed mean) is 3.6%. After the data, all four big banks expect the RBA to raise rates to 4.85% on 3 November, and markets priced about 90% odds, though none expects another rise in December. The economy is softening: 39,300 jobs lost in September, unemployment 4.7%, flat household spending and weak business confidence (NAB −13). China’s factories slipped back into contraction in October, a risk for Australian exports. Next: RBA decision and forecasts 3 Nov (UK 03:30), household spending 4 Nov, trade 5 Nov.
stories.NZD: The RBNZ surprised markets on 28 October by holding at 2.75% when a rise to 3.00% was expected; the vote was 4–3. The majority pointed to softer inflation (3.7% in Q3, from 4.1%), weak wage growth and the risk of a global slowdown. But the bank still expects to raise rates later and sees inflation rising to 4.4% in the December quarter because of fuel, and most banks now expect a rise on 9 December. The economy is weak (GDP +0.2% in Q2, unemployment 5.6%, a trade deficit of NZ$1.97bn in September), though business confidence edged up and card spending is 6.9% higher than a year ago. Next: Q3 jobs report 3 Nov (UK 21:45; unemployment 5.5% expected), general election 7 Nov.
stories.CHF: Switzerland is the outlier: inflation is only 1.0% (September, a two-year high on heating oil and fuel), and the SNB holds at 0% and stands ready to sell francs if needed. The franc is a safe haven that tends to gain when global worries rise. The economy is strong: GDP jumped 1.5% in Q2 (1.9% including big sporting events), factories are still expanding (PMI 55.3), shoppers are spending (retail +3.2% on a year) and unemployment is low at 3.1%. Next: retail sales and factory survey 2 Nov, October inflation 3 Nov (0.0% on the month expected), unemployment and a speech by SNB chair Schlegel 5 Nov; the next SNB decision is in December.
stories.CNY: China is shown because it drives AUD, NZD and commodity demand. Growth picked up to 4.5% on a year in Q3, from 4.3%, meeting the 4.5–5% target thanks mostly to exports (trade surplus $133.5bn in September). But October surveys were weak: the official factory index fell to 49.3 from 50.1 (below 50 means shrinking), as export orders dropped after Christmas orders were rushed out in September, and services and construction slipped to 49.7. Demand at home is soft (retail sales +1.1%) as the property slump continues, inflation is low (0.9%) and lending rates were left at 3.00%. Some economists are calling for more government support. Next: no big Chinese releases on the calendar in the coming week.

oil.title: Oil (WTI and Brent)
oil.what: The price of crude oil. Brent is the global benchmark, WTI the US one.
oil.now: Brent settled at $117.64 on 30 Oct (the contract that expired that day) and WTI at $104.12, six-month highs. That is roughly where prices were in late April, but up about 60% from the late-June low near $72, and about 14% in October alone. The Iran conflict is the driver: Houthi attacks on Saudi refineries, a tanker hit in the Strait of Hormuz and fears of US strikes on Iran after the 3 Nov midterms. Progress in Qatar-led talks, higher Saudi and Russian exports, or any easing would pull prices back.
oil.links: High oil helps oil exporters (CAD) and hurts importers (JPY, EUR). It feeds straight into inflation, which is why central banks have turned to raising rates.

gold.title: Gold
gold.what: Gold priced in US dollars. It pays no interest, so it competes with what investors can earn elsewhere.
gold.now: Down about 13% in six months, at around $4,030, and it has dipped below $4,000 at times in the past week. High oil keeps inflation worries and rate-rise bets alive (markets see about an 85% chance of a Fed rise in December), which keeps real interest rates high (US 10-year after inflation about 2.6%). Central-bank buying and safe-haven demand during the Middle East conflict are the support.
gold.links: Gold tends to rise when real yields fall, the dollar weakens or fear spikes. It often moves with CHF and JPY as a safe haven, and with AUD, since Australia is a big producer.

silver.title: Silver
silver.what: Half precious metal, half industrial metal (solar panels, electronics), so it swings more than gold.
silver.now: Down about 29% in six months, roughly double gold’s fall, at around $52: the same rate headwind, plus worries about factory demand as growth slows (China’s factory index fell back below 50 in October).
silver.links: Follows gold in direction but with bigger swings; weaker Chinese industry weighs on it.
